Chapter 5. Tailoring Reading Approaches to Different Types of Books.
You know, not every book is meant to be read the same way. Just like a chef wouldn’t use the same knife for every ingredient, we can’t expect one reading style to fit every kind of book. The trick is to match your approach to the type of book in your hands.
Let’s start with practical books—think manuals, self-help guides, or how-to texts. These books are all about helping you solve problems or learn new skills. The real goal here? Figure out what the author’s recommending, and see how you can put it into practice.
So, what’s the best way to get the most out of a practical book? First, ask yourself—what problem is this book trying to tackle? Then, get really clear about the solutions it’s offering. Are the steps doable for you, or do they feel out of reach? And here’s where it gets interesting: actually try out the advice. Notice what works and what doesn’t. It’s a cycle—read, apply, learn, and repeat. That’s how you really absorb what these books have to offer.
Now, what about imaginative literature? Novels, plays, poetry—these are a completely different experience. Here, you’re not just looking for advice or instructions. You’re stepping into another world, letting yourself be swept along by stories and emotions.
When you read imaginative works, let yourself get lost in the story. Follow the characters, feel their highs and lows. Keep an eye out for patterns—maybe a certain image keeps popping up, or there’s a theme that keeps resurfacing. Ask yourself, how does this story make you feel? Does it remind you of something in your own life, or maybe something everyone can relate to? And don’t forget—talk about it with others. Sharing your thoughts can open up new perspectives and deepen your appreciation.
Then there are books that dive into history, science, or philosophy—these can be a bit more demanding, but so rewarding. Each one needs its own strategy.
For history books, focus on the flow of events—what happened, why, and who was involved? Try to spot any biases or missing pieces in the story. With science, really pay attention to how things are defined. Look at the evidence, the way experiments are set up, and what’s actually proven versus what’s just a theory. And when you’re reading philosophy, roll up your sleeves. You’ll need to dig into arguments, question definitions, and wrestle with big ideas that might not have simple answers.
No matter which of these genres you’re tackling, some habits always pay off. Take notes, jot down summaries, and ask yourself questions if something’s not clear. If you get stuck, look for other sources, and don’t be shy about sharing your thoughts with others. Sometimes a conversation is the best way to check your understanding.
So, here’s the key takeaway—when you adjust how you read to fit the kind of book you’re exploring, you get more out of it. Not only will you understand more, but you’ll also find reading way more enjoyable and rewarding.
